title: Esther 2:8–18
context: The king’s commandment is heard, many maidens are gathered to Susa under Hegai, and Esther is taken into the king’s house. She obtains kindness from Hegai, is given cosmetics, food, and seven maidens, and is moved to the best place in the women’s house. Mordecai has instructed her not to make known her people or her relatives, and he walks daily before the court to learn how she is. Each young woman’s turn to go in to the king comes after twelve months of preparations; she goes in the evening and returns the next day to the second house, under Shaashgaz, who kept the concubines, and comes in no more unless the king calls her by name. When Esther’s turn comes, in the tenth month, Tebeth, in the seventh year of the reign, she requires only what Hegai advises, obtains favor, and the king loves her more than the others, sets the royal crown on her head, and makes her queen instead of Vashti. The king holds Esther’s feast, proclaims a holiday, and gives gifts. The unit is Esther’s rise and should be kept intact and told soberly, including the night with the king, without prurience and without modern culture-war framing. Her concealment of her people is a narrative fact under Mordecai’s instruction; the text does not pause to judge it here. Moral evaluations of that concealment, as prudence in a dangerous court or as a troubling silence, have been offered within both traditions and should be named only as hedged options, not as a party contrast. The book never names God. Hidden-providence readings of her favor and her crowning are common in both traditions and remain shared ground, held with a light hand, not as a code in Hegai’s kindness or in the month name. Both traditions read the unit as the making of a Jewish queen whose people are still hidden.

verses.text: So, when the king’s commandment and his decree was heard, and when many maidens were gathered together to the citadel of Susa, to the custody of Hegai, Esther was taken into the king’s house, to the custody of Hegai, keeper of the women.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the commandment and decree are heard, many maidens are gathered to the citadel of Susa, to Hegai’s custody, and “Esther was taken into the king’s house, to the custody of Hegai, keeper of the women.” The verb is that she was taken; the notes do not recast the gathering as a freely chosen contest, and they also do not press a later slogan onto the line. She enters the same house already described in 2:3.

Arminian readers take the taking as a real removal into the king’s house, Esther now inside a process she did not design.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the wording: the decree is heard, the maidens are gathered, and Esther is taken into Hegai’s custody, the path by which she will come before the king.

Both traditions tell the entry soberly, without a contrast over her degree of choice, which the verse does not settle at length.

verses.text: The maiden pleased him, and she obtained kindness from him. He quickly gave her cosmetics and her portions of food, and the seven choice maidens who were to be given her out of the king’s house. He moved her and her maidens to the best place in the women’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
The maiden pleases Hegai, and “she obtained kindness from him.” Hegai quickly gives her cosmetics, her portions of food, and seven choice maidens, and moves her and her maidens to the best place in the women’s house. The favor is Hegai’s, stated as kindness, and the notes do not turn it into a revealed sign or deny that later readers often see providence in such favor. That larger reading remains shared and hedged.

Arminian readers take the kindness as a real turn in the women’s house, Hegai acting promptly for Esther, a human favor with large effects.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from what is written: she pleased him, she obtained kindness, and she was placed in the best part of the house. A hidden-providence reading of that kindness belongs to the book as a whole, not to a secret word in this verse.

Both traditions refuse to decode the cosmetics and the seven maidens, and they invent no contrast over Hegai’s favor.

verses.text: Esther had not made known her people nor her relatives, because Mordecai had instructed her that she should not make it known.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Esther had not made known her people nor her relatives, because Mordecai had instructed her that she should not make it known.” The concealment is narrated as obedience to Mordecai’s instruction. The book does not pause here to praise or blame it. Within both traditions some have read the silence as prudence in a foreign court; some have found it morally uneasy. Those evaluations should stay hedged. They do not amount to an Arminian–Reformed fork, and they should not be forced into one.

Arminian readers take the concealment as a real choice under instruction, a fact of the plot, and they refuse to settle its moral quality as if this verse had judged it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the silence as the narrative gives it: her people and her relatives are not made known, because Mordecai had so instructed her. Later chapters will test that silence; this line only reports it.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the concealment and keep moral comment, if any, modest and unpartisan.

verses.text: Mordecai walked every day in front of the court of the women’s house, to find out how Esther was doing, and what would become of her.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Mordecai walked every day in front of the court of the women’s house, to find out how Esther was doing, and what would become of her.” Mordecai remains near, day after day, without being inside the house. The verse shows care and watchfulness, and a real uncertainty about what will become of her.

Arminian readers take the daily walk as a genuine, costly attention, Mordecai seeking news of the daughter he has raised, not yet knowing the outcome.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a fatherly watch at the court of the women’s house, every day, until the turn of 2:15–17 will answer, in part, what is to become of her.

Both traditions keep the line as family care in a dangerous place, without reading a hidden divine name out of the daily walk.

verses.text: Each young woman’s turn came to go in to King Ahasuerus after her purification for twelve months (for so were the days of their purification accomplished, six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with sweet fragrances and with preparations for beautifying women).
verses.arminianNotes:
Each young woman’s turn to go in to the king comes after her purification for twelve months, six months with oil of myrrh and six with sweet fragrances and preparations for beautifying women. The long preparation is the court’s custom as the book tells it. The notes describe it briefly and soberly, without lingering on the toilette and without using it as a modern example.

Arminian readers take the twelve months as a real waiting and preparation required of the gathered young women, including Esther, before any of them goes in.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the six and six months as the stated custom, a year of preparations, not a symbol of some other purification.

Both traditions refuse prurience and refuse allegory, and they invent no contrast over the custom.

verses.text: The young woman then came to the king like this: whatever she desired was given her to go with her out of the women’s house to the king’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the young woman comes to the king, “whatever she desired was given her to go with her out of the women’s house to the king’s house.” She may take what she wants from the women’s house for that going in. The verse is a rule of the procession, told without further detail.

Arminian readers take the permission as a real court custom, each candidate provided for the journey from one house to the other.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the line as the stated procedure: whatever she desired was given her to take with her. Esther’s own choice, in 2:15, will stand out against this background.

Both traditions tell it soberly and do not fill in the desired things the verse leaves unnamed.

verses.text: In the evening she went, and on the next day she returned into the second women’s house, to the custody of Shaashgaz, the king’s eunuch, who kept the concubines. She came in to the king no more, unless the king delighted in her, and she was called by name.
verses.arminianNotes:
“In the evening she went, and on the next day she returned into the second women’s house, to the custody of Shaashgaz, the king’s eunuch, who kept the concubines. She came in to the king no more, unless the king delighted in her, and she was called by name.” The night with the king is stated, and so is the ordinary sequel: the second house, and no return unless she is called. The notes report that arrangement plainly and briefly, without prurience and without a culture-war frame.

Arminian readers take the evening and the next day as the real path most of these young women walked, a night that ordinarily ended in the house of the concubines.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also stay with the wording: Shaashgaz kept the concubines, and a further coming in depended on the king’s delight and a call by name. The verse is hard, and it should be told as it is written.

Both traditions refuse to sensationalize the night or to moralize it into a separate debate, and they invent no contrast over it.

verses.text: Now when the turn of Esther, the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her for his daughter, came to go in to the king, she required nothing but what Hegai the king’s eunuch, the keeper of the women, advised. Esther obtained favor in the sight of all those who looked at her.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the turn of Esther comes, “the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her for his daughter,” she requires “nothing but what Hegai the king’s eunuch, the keeper of the women, advised.” She obtains favor in the sight of all who look at her. The family notice repeats 2:7 and names her father Abihail. Her only request is Hegai’s advice, against the wider permission of 2:13.

Arminian readers take that restraint as a real choice in the moment, and the favor as a genuine welcome, without forcing a moral of humility onto every detail.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note Abihail, the adopted daughter, and the decision to take only Hegai’s advice. Favor in the sight of all is the verse’s own report; a providence reading of that favor remains shared and hedged.

Both traditions keep the line in the rise of Esther and invent no contrast over her request.

verses.text: So Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus into his royal house in the tenth month, which is the month Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign.
verses.arminianNotes:
Esther is taken to King Ahasuerus in his royal house “in the tenth month, which is the month Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign.” The date is precise: Tebeth, the seventh year, four years after the feast of the third year in 1:3. The notes do not fill the interval with a campaign history the verse does not give. If Ahasuerus is the Xerxes of the common identification, that identification remains hedged, as already said at 1:1.

Arminian readers take the month and the year as a real date in the reign, the night of Esther’s going in fixed in the calendar of the court.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep Tebeth and the seventh year as the narrative’s own timing, and they refuse to build a larger Persian chronology as if it had been written here.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the date and do not decode the month name.

verses.text: The king loved Esther more than all the women, and she obtained favor and kindness in his sight more than all the virgins; so that he set the royal crown on her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The king loved Esther more than all the women, and she obtained favor and kindness in his sight more than all the virgins; so that he set the royal crown on her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti.” The rise is complete in this line: love, favor, kindness, the crown, and the place left empty in chapter 1. The book still does not name God. Hidden-providence readings of the crowning are common in both traditions and should be held as a reading of the whole story, not as a proof packed into the king’s love.

Arminian readers take the love and the crown as a real royal choice, Esther made queen instead of Vashti, a human decision with a long public sequel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from the king’s love and the favor she obtained, the crown set on her head. That God is not named here does not prove that he is absent, and it also does not turn the crown into a coded sign.

Both traditions share a hedged providence reading of her rise, and they invent no party contrast over the silence or the crown.

verses.text: Then the king made a great feast for all his princes and his servants, even Esther’s feast; and he proclaimed a holiday in the provinces, and gave gifts according to the king’s bounty.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king makes “a great feast for all his princes and his servants, even Esther’s feast”; he proclaims a holiday in the provinces, and gives gifts according to his bounty. The new queen is announced in the same register as the feasts of chapter 1, now named as Esther’s feast, with a holiday and gifts. The unit closes on that public honor, her people still unnamed at court.

Arminian readers take the feast, the holiday, and the gifts as a real royal celebration of the new queen, the rise now visible across the provinces.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a public close: Esther’s feast, a holiday, and gifts according to the king’s bounty, the court marking what 2:17 has done.

Both traditions end the rise here, still without a contrast over concealment or over the book’s silence about God, and without turning the holiday into a type of a later feast before the book itself does so.
